description: We are a team of enthusiastic students passionate about science, technology, and innovation. We enjoy exploring data, solving problems, and learning together. Though we may not be climate scientists just yet, we are eager to uncover environmental trends and turn complex data into meaningful insights. 🌍🚀
summary:
EarthScope is an interactive platform for exploring how Pakistan’s environment has changed over time. We built it for NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026’s “Be an Earth System Trend Detective!” challenge, using six monthly indicators from NASA’s MERRA-2 and GLDAS-2.1 datasets: 2-meter air temperature, surface skin temperature, precipitation, evapotranspiration, topsoil moisture, and rootzone moisture.

With EarthScope, users can trace historical patterns, compare any month against its seasonal baseline, spot unusual conditions, check whether a trend is statistically significant, and see how variables move together. The platform also projects indicators forward, with uncertainty intervals shown alongside every forecast.

Under the hood, we built a monthly data-processing pipeline, applied the Mann-Kendall test and Sen’s slope for trend detection, and compared five forecasting methods on a chronological holdout, so each model was judged on the most recent data it had not seen during training.

Our goal was to make complex Earth-system records approachable without hiding how the results are produced. Methods, results, and limitations stay visible throughout.
details:
About EarthScope

Environmental data is easy to find. Understanding what it says about long-term change is much harder. EarthScope was built to close that gap.

We developed it for NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 and its “Be an Earth System Trend Detective!” challenge. It brings historical analysis, statistical trend detection, anomaly exploration, and machine-learning forecasting into one interactive platform. Our first focus is Pakistan, using monthly, area-averaged records for the primary period from 2001 to 2025.

Environmental Data

EarthScope draws on six indicators from two NASA products.

NASA MERRA-2

  • 2-Meter Air Temperature (°C)
  • Surface Skin Temperature (°C)
  • Bias-Corrected Precipitation (mm/month)

NASA GLDAS-2.1 Noah Land Surface Model

  • Total Evapotranspiration (mm/month)
  • Topsoil Moisture, 0–10 cm (kg/m²)
  • Rootzone Moisture, 10–40 cm (kg/m²)

Together they cover both atmospheric and land-surface behavior in a single analytical platform.

How the Platform Works

We start by collecting NASA-derived records and standardizing them into monthly time series. Each series is checked for missing values, date ordering, numerical validity, unit consistency, metadata, and geographic coverage.

Once the data is prepared, EarthScope explores seasonal patterns, statistical distributions, unusual observations, and relationships between variables.

To find anomalies, we use a 2001–2020 monthly climatology as the baseline. Each month is compared with the baseline for the same calendar month, so unusual conditions stand apart from normal seasonal swings.

For long-term trends, we implemented linear regression, the Mann–Kendall test, Sen’s slope, Yue–Pilon trend-free pre-whitening, and Seasonal Mann–Kendall testing where appropriate.

Our analysis found statistically significant increasing trends in precipitation, evapotranspiration, topsoil moisture, and rootzone moisture. Surface skin temperature shows a decreasing trend, while 2-meter air temperature shows no statistically significant monotonic trend at the 0.05 level. These results describe national area-averaged behavior. They should not be read as uniform change across every location in Pakistan.

Machine-Learning Forecasting

EarthScope also produces monthly multi-step forecasts. Rather than rely on a single algorithm, we compared five approaches: Persistence, Seasonal Naive, Linear Drift, Ridge Regression, and Random Forest Regression.

The forecasting pipeline uses historical lags, rolling statistics, seasonal Fourier features, and time-trend information. To keep the evaluation honest, we split the data chronologically into training and holdout periods instead of shuffling observations. For each environmental variable, the recommended model is the one with the lowest holdout RMSE.

The public interface shows projections alongside historical values, with 95% uncertainty intervals. Forecasts are presented as ranges, not as certain outcomes.

Software and Technology

EarthScope combines modern web tools with a scientific computing stack.

  • Frontend: Next.js 14, React 18, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, and Lucide React
  • Backend: Python, FastAPI, Pydantic, and Uvicorn
  • Scientific computing and machine learning: Pandas, NumPy, SciPy, scikit-learn, PyMannKendall, PyArrow, Joblib, and Matplotlib
  • Testing: Pytest, pytest-asyncio, and frontend testing and build-validation scripts

The backend exposes structured API services for historical data, trend analysis, anomaly analysis, forecasting, model metrics, and geographic summaries. The frontend presents these results through an interactive interface.

What Makes EarthScope Different?

Most tools show a chart or a prediction. EarthScope connects the whole chain of an environmental investigation. Users can move from historical observations to seasonal anomalies, statistical trends, relationships between variables, and future projections without leaving the platform.

It also shows how each result was produced, including methodology, model evaluation metrics, data provenance, and limitations. Users can see what a result says and how it was reached.

During development, we worked through differences in measurement units, seasonal cycles, extreme precipitation events, autocorrelation, data leakage in model evaluation, geographic resolution, and forecast uncertainty. We also aimed to make the technical results understandable to people without a specialist background.

Potential Impact and Current Limitations

EarthScope can help students, researchers, environmental analysts, and anyone curious about Pakistan’s environmental history. It gives them an accessible starting point for investigating historical patterns and seeing how different Earth-system indicators relate to one another.

It also has clear limits. The current geographic explorer is a data-informed schematic, not a full high-resolution GIS system. Forecasts are based on historical behavior, and national averages cannot capture every local condition. EarthScope is an analytical and educational platform, not an operational early-warning system.

Our goal is to make environmental evidence easier to explore, interpret, and question, with the underlying science and its limitations in plain view.

Project Access, Source Code & Documentation

  1. Live Application: https://earth-system-trend-detective-lyart.vercel.app/
    Try the deployed EarthScope platform and its interactive analysis features.
  2. GitHub Repository (Source Code): https://github.com/fasitahir/earth-system-trend-detective.git
    Frontend and backend source code and development resources.
  3. Project Documentation (Technical Report): https://drive.google.com/file/d/1zxAWQtfO2wjq85ZngqKfGTuEP_zAJoBW/view?usp=drive_link
    The full project report: architecture, NASA data sources, data processing, statistical methods, machine-learning models, evaluation results, implementation, findings, and limitations.
  4. NASA Datasets: https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1hI8t9x1OdY3sSqpFRN25mPyEbr8ad6iX?usp=drive_link
    The NASA datasets used in the analysis.
